exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 1 and 2, you may assume that $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{4} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \\ {- 4} \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 5 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ {- 4} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{4} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 3} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 10 \\ {- 8} \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Write $$\textbf{x}$$ as the sum of two vectors, one in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \right\}$$ and the other in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{4} \right\}$$ .

$$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 1 \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ {- 2} \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{4} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 5 \\ {- 2} \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Write $$\mathbf{v}$$ as the sum of two vectors, one in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \right\}$$ and the other in $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{3} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{4} \right\}$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 3–6, verify that $$\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set, and then find the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$\text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 4 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. - 1 1 0 \left]\right.$$

$$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 3 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 4 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. - 4 3 0 \left]\right.$$

$$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 2 \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 1} \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. 1 - 1 - 2 \left]\right.$$

$$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 4} \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. 0 1 1 \left]\right.$$

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 7–10, let $$W$$ be the subspace spanned by the $$\mathbf{u}’s$$ , and write $$\textbf{y}$$ as the sum of a vector in $$W$$ and a vector orthogonal to $$W$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 3 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. 5 1 4 \left]\right.$$

$$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 4 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left[\right. - 1 3 - 2 \left]\right.$$

$$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 3 \\ 1 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{3} = \left[\right. - 1 0 1 1 \left]\right.$$

$$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 4 \\ 5 \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{3} = \left[\right. 0 - 1 1 - 1 \left]\right.$$

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 11 and 12, find the closest point to $$\textbf{y}$$ in the subspace $$W$$ spanned by $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 1 \\ 5 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 1 \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 1 - 1 1 - 1 \left]\right.$$

$$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 13 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 2} \\ {- 1} \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. - 4 1 0 3 \left]\right.$$

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 13 and 14, find the best approximation to $$\textbf{z}$$ by vectors of the form $$c_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$\textbf{z} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 7} \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 1} \\ {- 3} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 1 1 0 - 1 \left]\right.$$

$$\textbf{z} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 4 \\ 0 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 0 \\ {- 1} \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. 5 - 2 4 2 \left]\right.$$

Let $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 9} \\ 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ {- 5} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Find the distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to the plane in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ .

Let $$\textbf{y}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ be as in Exercise 12. Find the distance from $$\textbf{y}$$ to the subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ spanned by $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ .

Let $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 8 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {2/3} \\ {1/3} \\ {2/3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2/3} \\ {2/3} \\ {1/3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ .

Let $$\textbf{y} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 9 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {1/\sqrt{10}} \\ {- 3/\sqrt{10}} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$W = \text{Span} \left{\right. \mathbf{u}_{1} \left.\right} .$$

list.item: Let $$U$$ be the $$2 \times 1$$ matrix whose only column is $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ . Compute $$U^{T} U$$ and $$UU^{T}$$ .

problem.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{u}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{u}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 1} \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\mathbf{u}_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Note that $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ are orthogonal but that $$\mathbf{u}_{3}$$ is not orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ or $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ . It can be shown that $$\mathbf{u}_{3}$$ is not in the subspace $$W$$ spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ . Use this fact to construct a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ that is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ .

Let $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ be as in Exercise 19, and let $$\mathbf{u}_{4} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . It can be shown that $$\mathbf{u}_{4}$$ is not in the subspace $$W$$ spanned by $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ . Use this fact to construct a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ that is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 21–30, all vectors and subspaces are in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$\textbf{z}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and to $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ and if $$W = \text{Span} \left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{2} \right\}$$ , then $$\textbf{z}$$ must be in $$W^{\bot}$$ .
(T/F) For each $$\textbf{y}$$ and each subspace $$W$$ , the vector $$\textbf{y} - \text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ is orthogonal to $$W$$ .
(T/F) The orthogonal projection $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto a subspace $$W$$ can sometimes depend on the orthogonal basis for $$W$$ used to compute $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ .
(T/F) If $$\textbf{y}$$ is in a subspace $$W$$ , then the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ is $$\textbf{y}$$ itself.
(T/F) The best approximation to $$\textbf{y}$$ by elements of a subspace $$W$$ is given by the vector $$\textbf{y} - \text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y}$$ .
(T/F) If $$W$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and if $$\mathbf{v}$$ is in both $$W$$ and $$W^{\bot}$$ , then $$\mathbf{v}$$ must be the zero vector.
(T/F) In the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem, each term in formula (2) for $$\widehat{\textbf{y}}$$ is itself an orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto a subspace of $$W$$ .

(T/F) If $$\textbf{y} = \textbf{z}_{1} + \textbf{z}_{2}$$ , where $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ is in a subspace $$W$$ and $$\textbf{z}_{2}$$ is in $$W^{\bot}$$ , then $$\textbf{z}_{1}$$ must be the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto $$W$$ .
(T/F) If the columns of an $$n \times p$$ matrix $$U$$ are orthonormal, then $$UU^{T}{\textbf{y}}$$ is the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{y}$$ onto the column space of $$U$$ .
(T/F) If an $$n \times p$$ matrix $$U$$ has orthonormal columns, then $$UU^{T}\textbf{x} = \textbf{x}$$ for all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

Let $$A$$ be an $$m \times n$$ matrix. Prove that every vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ can be written in the form $$\textbf{x} = \textbf{p} + \mathbf{u}$$ , where $$\textbf{p}$$ is in $$\text{Row} A$$ and $$\mathbf{u}$$ is in $$\text{Nul} A$$ . Also, show that if the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is consistent, then there is a unique $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\text{Row} A$$ such that $$A\textbf{p} = \textbf{b}$$ .

Let $$W$$ be a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ with an orthogonal basis $$\left\{ \textbf{w}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{w}_{p} \right\}$$ , and let $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{q} \right\}$$ be an orthogonal basis for $$W^{\bot}$$ .

list.item: Explain why $$\left\{ \textbf{w}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \textbf{w}_{p} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \ldots \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{q} \right\}$$ is an orthogonal set.
Explain why the set in part (a) spans $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 33–36, first change the given pattern into a vector $$\textbf{w}$$ of zeros and ones and then use the method illustrated in Example 5 to find a matrix $$M$$ so that $$\mathbf{w}^{T}M\mathbf{w} = 0$$ , but $$\mathbf{u}^{T}M\mathbf{u} \neq 0$$ for all other nonzero vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ of zeros and ones.

problem.paragraph: [T] Let $$U$$ be the $$8 \times 4$$ matrix in Exercise 43 in Section 6.2. Find the closest point to $$\textbf{y} = \left( 1 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 1 \right)$$ in $$\text{Col} U$$ . Write the keystrokes or commands you use to solve this problem.
[T] Let $$U$$ be the matrix in Exercise 37. Find the distance from $$\mathbf{b} = \left( {1,1,1,1, - 1, - 1, - 1, - 1} \right)$$ to $$\text{Col} U$$ .

problem.paragraph: Compute $$\text{proj} _{\textit{w}} \textbf{y} & = & \frac{\textbf{y}\cdot\textbf{u}_{1}}{\textbf{u}_{1} \cdot\textbf{u}_{1}} \textbf{u}_{1} + \frac{\textbf{y}\cdot\textbf{u}_{2}}{\textbf{u}_{2} \cdot\textbf{u}_{2}} \textbf{u}_{2} = \frac{88}{66} \textbf{u}_{1} + \frac{- 2}{6} \textbf{u}_{2} & = & \frac{4}{3} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 7 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 1 \\ - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 9 \\ 1 \\ 6\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = y$$

In this case, $$\textbf{y}$$ happens to be a linear combination of $$\mathbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{u}_{2}$$ , so $$\textbf{y}$$ is in $$W$$ . The closest point in $$W$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ is $$\textbf{y}$$ itself.

Using Theorem 10, let $$U$$ be a matrix whose columns consist of an orthonormal basis for $$W$$ . Then $$\text{proj} _{W}\textbf{z} = UU^{T}\textbf{z} = UU^{T}(\textbf{x} + \textbf{y}) = UU^{T}\textbf{x} + UU^{T}\textbf{y} = \text{proj} _{W}\textbf{x} + \text{proj} _{W}\textbf{y} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ .
